Unit 0 · Start here How this tutor works Every exercise on this site runs against a real git repository in your browser. Nothing is simulated, and nothing you type can hurt anything. Before you start You've used git — you commit, branch, push, and you've googled your way out of at least one mess. That's the level this course starts from. It spends its time on the half of git that most people never get taught: rewriting history on purpose, the object database underneath, digging through the past, and the collaboration commands that stop you losing other people's work. The idea The awkward thing about learning advanced git is that the interesting commands are the frightening ones. Nobody wants to practise rebase --onto on the repository they get paid to look after, so most people learn these commands the hard way — at 6pm, on a branch that matters, from a Stack Overflow answer written in 2013. b: Unit 0 · Start here The one mental model Four sentences of theory that make every command in the four units after this one predictable instead of memorised. Before you start Nothing beyond having used git. If you can already say what a branch is made of, skim to Try it and move on. The idea Here it is, all of it: The whole model A commit is a complete snapshot of your project, plus a pointer to the commit that came before it. A branch is a sticky note with one commit's name on it. HEAD is a sticky note saying which branch you're standing on. Almost every git command is a way of moving one of those notes. Two consequences do most of the work in this course. Commits are snapshots, not diffs. Git shows you diffs because diffs are what humans want to read, but it stores whole trees. When you hear that a rebase "replays your changes", what actually happens is that git computes a diff between two snapshots, applies it somewhere else, and stores the resulting snapshot. The diff is a means, not the data. History points backwards. A commit names its parent; a parent knows nothing about its children. So "the commits on this branch" is never a list git looks up — it's the answer to a walk, starting at the sticky note and following parents until it runs out. Everything follows from that: Deleting a branch deletes a sticky note. The commits are untouched — they have simply become unreachable , which is why they can be recovered. You cannot edit a commit. Its name is a hash of its contents, parent included, so changing anything makes a different commit. Every "rewrite" command builds new commits and moves a sticky note to them. Changing one commit changes every commit after it, because each one's hash includes its parent's hash. Rewriting the tip is cheap; rewriting the root rewrites everything. Try it The sandbox below has two branches. Watch what git branch -D does and doesn't destroy — the goals check that the commits outlived the branch that named them. Useful here: git log -

No name, no permissions, no history. tree a list of entries: mode name id . A commit object that no ref reaches is exactly what "dangling" means, and you can create one on purpose here. This split is not trivia. b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing Objects and hashes Git is a key-value store where the key is the hash of the value. Once you have typed that hash out by hand, half of git's behaviour stops being surprising. The idea Git stores four kinds of object : a blob (a file's contents), a tree (a directory listing), a commit, and an annotated tag . Each one is stored under a key, and the key is the SHA-1 hash of the object itself. That's the whole storage layer. The hash isn't taken over the file's bytes alone. Git prefixes a header — the type, a space, the length in bytes, and a zero byte — and hashes the lot: sha1("blob " + <length> + "\0" + <contents>) So a 12-byte file containing hello world\n is hashed as the 17 bytes blob 12\0hello world\n . You can reproduce this outside git with any SHA-1 tool, and people do, as a sanity check. Being content-addressed has consequences you rely on daily: Identical content is stored once, however many commits or branches contain it. An id cannot lie about what it names. Corruption is detectable: rehash the object and compare. Nothing can be edited in place. Every command that appears to modify history actually writes new objects — which is why so much of what looks destroyed is merely unnamed. Try it Type this in the sandbox and watch the id show up as a filename: echo "hello world" > hello.txt git hash-object hello.txt # compute the id, store nothing git hash-object -w hello.txt # compute it and write the object ls .git/objects/ # the first two hex characters are the directory git cat-file -t <paste the id> # what type is it? git cat-file -p <paste the id> # print it back Note what did not happen: nothing was committed, nothing was staged, and git status still shows an untracked file. You put an object in the database directly. b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing Refs, HEAD and symbolic refs Branches are one-line text files. Once you have edited one with echo, the difference between checkout, reset and branch -f stops mattering very much. The idea An object id is 40 characters of hex, so git gives you names for the ones you care about. A ref is a name holding one object id, stored as a file: .git/refs/heads/main → a branch .git/refs/tags/v1.0 → a tag .git/refs/remotes/origin/main → a remote-tracking ref Each contains one line: a 40-character id and a newline. That's it. A branch is not a container, a list, or a lineage — it is a filename with a hash in it. HEAD is the interesting one, because it usually doesn't contain an id at all: $ cat .git/HEAD ref: refs/heads/main That's a symbolic ref — a ref pointing at another ref. It's the indirection that makes committing work: git commit updates whatever ref HEAD names, so the branch moves and HEAD follows for free. b: Unit 1 · Internals & plumbing The index, properly The index isn't a queue of changes — it's a complete proposed snapshot. That one correction fixes most confusion about staging. The idea People picture the index as a list of changes waiting to be committed. It is actually a full flat list of every path in your project, each with a blob id and some cached file stats: $ git ls-files -s 100644 8d0e41234f24b6da002d962a26c2495ea16a425f 0 README.md 100644 151e2f818f2f6a619a0049dec48becf86b836ca7 0 count.py Read that as a proposed tree. git commit doesn't gather your changes; it turns the index into a tree object and points a commit at it. That's why git write-tree works at any moment, and why an empty git add session still produces a complete snapshot. So git status is two comparisons against this middle thing: index vs HEAD "Changes to be committed" working tree vs index "Changes not staged for commit" in neither "Untracked files" And it explains the situation everyone hits: a file can appear in both lists at once. You staged version 2, then edited it into version 3. The index holds v2, disk holds v3, and committing gets you v2 — which is a feature, and the entire basis of git add -p . b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Amending the last commit git commit --amend doesn't edit your commit. It builds a replacement and abandons the original — and everything else in this unit is that same move, at larger scale. The idea You commit, then notice the typo. git commit --amend fixes it, and the mental model most people carry away is "amend edits the last commit". It can't. A commit's id is a hash of its contents, so an edited commit is a different commit. What actually happens: Git builds a new commit from the current index, with the same parent as the old one and whatever message you give. It moves your branch to the new commit. The old commit is now unreachable . It is still there, byte for byte, named in the reflog . Two useful consequences fall straight out. An amend is always recoverable — git reset --hard HEAD@{1} puts you back. And an amend is a rewrite : if you already pushed, your branch and the remote's now disagree about a commit that exists in both, which is why the next push is rejected. Try it git log --oneline git commit --amend -m "A better message" git log --oneline # same position, different id git reflog # both ids are here: the new one and the old git cat-file -p HEAD@{1} # the "gone" commit, still perfectly readable Amending content works the same way: stage something first, and it joins the replacement commit instead of becoming a new one. The details (open as much as you like) Amend keeps the author, replaces the committer The new commit inherits the original's author name, email and date, and gets you and now as committer . So git log still shows the original date while git log --format=%cd shows today. This is the same mechanism as cherry-pick and rebase — anything that replays a commit preserves authorship and records who moved it. b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Cherry-pick Copying one commit somewhere else. The mechanism is a three-way merge, which explains both why it usually just works and why the duplicate it leaves behind can bite you later. The idea You have a fix on one branch and you need it on another. git cherry-pick <commit> applies what that commit changed, here, and commits the result. "What that commit changed" is computed, not stored. Git does a three-way merge with: base the commit's parent — the world before it theirs the commit itself — the world after it ours where you are now That's why a cherry-pick can succeed even when the surrounding code has changed a lot: the merge only needs to reconcile the one region the commit touched. And it's why a conflict here looks exactly like a merge conflict — it is one. The result is a new commit with a new id : same author, same message, same tree change, different parent. The original stays where it was. You now have the same change twice in your project's history, under two names. Try it The sandbox has a hotfix branch with one commit you want on main : git log --oneline --all git checkout main git cherry-pick hotfix git log --oneline # a new id, the same subject git show HEAD # same change git cherry-pick -x hotfix~0 # try -x and read the message it writes The details (open as much as you like) -x, and why backports need it git cherry-pick -x appends a line to the message: (cherry picked from commit 961c4c8…) It costs nothing and it's the only durable record of where the change came from — the new commit has no structural link to the original. On a maintenance branch six months later, that line is the difference between "this was backported from main" and a mystery. Git doesn't do it by default because on a shared feature branch the referenced id may be one you rewrote away, making the note misleading. Opens that file in your editor. You change it. That's the whole "interactive" part. b: Unit 2 · History rewriting rebase --onto Rebase normally conflates two questions. --onto separates them: which commits to move, and where to put them. The idea git rebase main means two things at once: take the commits that aren't in main , and put them on top of main . Usually that's what you want, so the conflation goes unnoticed. It stops being what you want when your branch was started from the wrong place. Say you branched feature off feature-base , wrote three commits, and now feature-base is abandoned. A plain rebase onto main would replay everything not in main — including feature-base's commits, which you don't want. The three-argument form splits the question: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>] │ │ │ └── which commits: <upstream>..branch └── where they land So "move just my three commits onto main" is: git rebase --onto main feature-base feature Read it as: replay the commits after feature-base up to feature, on top of main. b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Rebase versus merge Not a matter of taste, exactly. They record different claims about what happened, and only one of them is safe on history other people have. The idea Your branch and main have both moved. You need them combined. Two options, and they differ in what ends up in the repository: merge one new merge commit with two parents. Your commits keep their ids. History records that two lines of work existed and were joined. rebase your commits are rebuilt on top of main, with new ids. History records a single line, as though you had started from today's main. So merge preserves what happened, and rebase presents what you wish had happened. Both are legitimate. The interesting question is not which is nicer to read but which facts you're prepared to lose. Where the answer is not a matter of taste: Unpushed local work: rebase freely. Nobody has those commits, so replacing them costs nothing, and you get a history that's reviewable. Anything others have based work on: merge. Rebasing changes the ids they're building on, and their next pull will try to reconcile two copies of every commit. A long-lived shared branch: merge, and stop asking. The "clean history" argument is not worth the recovery work. Try it The sandbox has diverged branches. h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Recovering with the reflog The reason none of this unit is dangerous. Every ref movement is written down, so almost every git accident is two commands from being undone. The idea Every time a ref moves, git appends a line to a log. HEAD's log is .git/logs/HEAD ; each branch has its own under .git/logs/refs/heads/ . A line looks like this: d1cf19b 587bc61 Ada Rivera <ada@example.com> 1709543400 +0000 commit: fix typo Old id, new id, who, when, why. That's the whole reflog — and because it records the id a ref moved away from , it is a list of every commit you have abandoned. So the recovery procedure for nearly everything is the same three steps: git reflog — read down the list until you recognise where you were. Note the id, or its HEAD@{n} address. git reset --hard <that> to go back, or git branch rescue <that> to give it a name without moving. The second option is the better instinct: putting a new branch on the lost commit can't make anything worse, and lets you look before you leap. Try it Destroy something, then get it back: git log --oneline git reset --hard HEAD~3 # three commits gone from the branch git log --oneline # confirmed gone git reflog # …and there they are git reset --hard HEAD@{1} # back git branch rescue HEAD@{2} # or name it instead of moving Then try the harder version: delete a branch entirely and recover it. The branch's own reflog goes with it, so you need HEAD's log — or git fsck . h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting reset versus revert Both undo. One rewrites history and one adds to it — and choosing wrong is how teams lose an afternoon. The idea Two questions, and the answers are unrelated: The distinction reset moves your branch to a different commit. History changes shape; the undone commits are no longer on the branch. revert makes a new commit that undoes an old one. History grows; nothing is removed. So the choice is not about safety — reset is perfectly safe on a branch nobody else has — it's about whether the commits are already somewhere else. If they are, reverting is the only honest option: rewriting would break everyone who already has them. The three resets reset takes a commit and moves up to three things to match it: --soft branch only index and worktree untouched, so the undone changes are all staged, ready to recommit --mixed branch + index the default. Changes survive in your files, unstaged --hard branch + index + worktree your files are overwritten. The one that discards work Two things it never does, both worth knowing precisely: it never touches untracked files (so reset --hard won't remove that build directory), and it never deletes commits from the object database (so the reflog can undo it). git reset --soft HEAD~3 is the useful one people don't know: three commits collapse into a fully staged change, and one git commit makes them one. That's a squash without a rebase. Try it git log --oneline git reset --soft HEAD~2 # look at git status: everything staged git reset --mixed HEAD # keep going: now unstaged git status git reset --hard HEAD # and now clean — the changes are gone from your files git reflog # every one of those moves is recorded git reset --hard HEAD@{3} # back to where you started The details (open as much as you like) Reverting a merge, and why it needs -m A merge commit has two parents, so "undo this commit" is ambiguous: undo relative to which side? git revert -m 1 <merge> keeps the first parent's line and undo

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting Rewriting published history Sometimes you have to. Here's how to do it with the least damage, and how to recognise the times you shouldn't. The idea The rule everyone repeats is "never rewrite published history". As stated it's too strong — the real content is: The actual rule Rewriting a branch replaces its commits with new ones. Anyone who has the old commits keeps them, and their git will try to combine both copies. So the cost of a rewrite is paid by everyone who already pulled — which is fine if that's nobody, or if you tell them. Which gives you a decision procedure rather than a taboo: Your own unpushed work Rewrite freely. Nobody is affected. Your own pushed feature branch, no one else on it Rewrite and push --force-with-lease . Normal practice. A shared feature branch Rewrite only after saying so. Everyone else needs git reset --hard origin/<branch> afterwards. main, or any long-lived branch Don't. Use revert . The exception that overrides all of it: a secret got committed. Then the history must be rewritten, everywhere, and the credential must be rotated anyway — because anyone who cloned already has it, and no rewrite can reach their disk. Rotate first; rewrite second. Try it The sandbox has a remote whose main has moved on, and a local branch you've rewritten. Watch git refuse, and then do it properly: git log --oneline --all git fetch git status # ahead and behind: you've diverged git push # rejected, and read the hint carefully git push --force # works, and would trample whatever origin had Then reset the sandbox and try the same thing with --force-with-lease instead, which is the subject of its own page because the difference matters so much. The details (open as much as you like) The message to send when you do rewrite a shared branch Rewrites go wrong socially, not technically. What people need is the exact command to run: I've rebased feature/parser and force-pushed. If you have it checked out: git fetch origin git reset

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 2 · History rewriting squash, fixup, autosquash The habit that makes review comments cheap: commit the fix now, marked for where it belongs, and let one rebase put everything in its place. The idea You're six commits into a branch and a reviewer points out a bug in the second one. The bad options are: amend the wrong commit, add a commit called "fix review comment" and leave the history messy, or stop everything and rebase interactively right now. The good option is a two-part habit. Now , commit the fix with a marker saying where it belongs: git commit --fixup=<the commit it fixes> which writes a commit whose subject is literally fixup! <that commit's subject> . You carry on working. Later , when you're ready to tidy up: git rebase -i --autosquash main Git reads the fixup! prefixes, moves each of those commits directly beneath the commit it names, and changes its command to fixup — before showing you the todo list. You confirm and it's done. Two variants: --fixup=X fold in, keep X's message. The everyday one --squash=X fold in, and combine both messages so you can edit them together Set git config --global rebase.autoSquash true and --autosquash becomes the default, at which point this is just how you work. Try it The sandbox already contains two marked commits — one fixup! and one squash! . Look at them, then let autosquash place them: git log --oneline git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5 # read the todo list carefully before saving: the lines have been reordered for you Compare it with git rebase -i HEAD~5 without --autosquash and see how much manual reordering you were spared. The details (open as much as you like) How git matches a fixup! to its target By subject text, not by id. fixup! Add the report attaches to the commit whose subject is Add the report . Consequences: Two commits with the same subject make the match ambiguous — git picks one, and it may not be yours. --fixup=<sha> is only a convenience for looking up that subject; what's stored is the tex

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 3 · Debugging & forensics bisect Ten questions to find one bad commit in a thousand. The command is easy; the skill is choosing a test that answers cleanly. The idea Something worked in March and doesn't now. There are 800 commits in between. Reading them is hopeless; binary search isn't: git bisect start git bisect bad # the current commit is broken git bisect good v2.1 # this one was fine # git checks out a commit halfway between. You test it. git bisect good # or: git bisect bad # …repeat. About 10 rounds for 800 commits. git bisect reset # back to where you were Each answer halves the range, so the cost is log₂(n) tests: 800 commits is ten. Git tracks the state in .git/BISECT_* and refs/bisect/* , checks out the midpoint for you, and at the end prints " <id> is the first bad commit ". What makes bisect work is the assumption that the property is monotone — good, good, good, bad, bad, bad. When it isn't (flaky test, a bug fixed and reintroduced), bisect will still give you an answer, and the answer will be wrong. That's the thing to be careful about, not the commands. Try it The sandbox has twelve commits. The tokenizer test passes at the start and fails at the tip; exactly one commit broke it. Find it: git log --oneline git bisect start git bisect bad git bisect good HEAD~11 cat tok.py # is the bug here? look at how it splits git bisect good # or bad # …keep going until git names the culprit git bisect reset The bug: at some point text.split() became text.split(" ") , which keeps an empty string when there are two spaces in a row. So your test each round is: does tok.py split on the literal " " ? The details (open as much as you like) bisect run — let a script answer If the test can be automated, don't sit through ten rounds: git bisect start HEAD HEAD~11 git bisect run python -m pytest tests/test_tok.py The convention is the shell one: exit 0 means good , anything from 1 to 124 means bad. Two special codes matter — 125 means "can't test this one, skip it"

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 3 · Debugging & forensics blame, moves and copies Plain git blame answers a slightly different question from the one you asked, and after any refactor the difference is the whole story. The idea git blame <file> tells you, for each line, the last commit that changed that line in that file . That last clause is the problem. Rename the file, move a function between files, or reindent the block, and every line's answer becomes the commit that did the moving — which is almost never who you're looking for. Three flags fix it, and they are the whole point of this page: -M detect lines moved within the file, and follow them past the move -C detect lines copied from other files modified in the same commit. Repeat it ( -C -C ) to search files that weren't modified too -w ignore whitespace, so a reindent stops hiding the author Habit worth forming: never run plain git blame . Run git blame -w -M -C , always. It's slower and it's right. Two more that narrow the question: -L 40,60 only those lines. Much faster on a large file <rev> -- <file> blame as of an older commit — what did this look like before the rewrite? Try it The sandbox has a file that was renamed, then split in two. Blame the reporting code and watch the answer change with the flags: git log --oneline git blame report.py # everything points at the split commit git blame -C report.py # …now the lines' real origin shows through git blame -M -C report.py git log --oneline -- report.py # only the commits git thinks touched this path The details (open as much as you like) Why rename detection is a guess Git stores no renames. A commit that renames a file stores a tree without the old path and with the new one — the "rename" is inferred later by comparing content similarity, and the threshold is configurable ( -M50% by default in diff). Consequence: a rename plus heavy editing in the same commit may not be detected at all, and splitting the change into two commits (rename, then edit) makes history much more legible

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 3 · Debugging & forensics fsck and dangling objects The last resort, and a genuinely useful one: everything in the database that nothing points at. The idea Git deletes objects only when gc runs, and gc only deletes objects nothing can reach. So between losing something and gc noticing, the object is still there — and git fsck is how you list what's in that state. git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs Two words that get used loosely and mean different things: unreachable no ref can get to it by walking parents and trees dangling unreachable, and nothing unreachable points at it either — so it's the tip of a lost chain Dangling is the more useful list: a lost branch of six commits produces six unreachable commits but only one dangling one, and that one is the tip you want to put a branch on. --no-reflogs is not optional in practice. By default the reflog counts as a starting point, so anything the reflog remembers is "reachable" and fsck stays quiet — which is exactly the case where you didn't need fsck anyway. Excluding reflogs shows what's genuinely orphaned. Try it This sandbox had a branch deleted. Compare what fsck says with and without reflogs, then rescue the work: git fsck --unreachable # quiet: the reflog still reaches them git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs # there they are git cat-file -p <one of the commit ids> git show <that id> # what was in it? git branch rescued <the newest one> # give it a name and it's history again The details (open as much as you like) Where lost work actually comes from A deleted branch the commits, plus the branch's own reflog, are gone. HEAD's log usually still names them Commits on a detached HEAD if HEAD was never on a branch, only HEAD's reflog knew — and once that expires, only fsck A dropped stash a stash is a commit; dropping it unreferences it. git fsck finds it and git stash apply <id> takes it back An abandoned rebase the pre-rebase chain, findable via ORIG_HEAD or the reflog first git add ed but never committed th

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 3 · Debugging & forensics The pickaxe Search history by content instead of by path: when did this string appear, and which commit took it out again? The idea git grep searches your working tree. The pickaxe searches history , and it comes in two flavours that answer different questions: -S<string> commits where the number of occurrences of that string changed — so, where it was introduced or removed -G<regex> commits whose diff mentions it at all, including lines merely moved around The distinction is sharper than it looks. Move a line containing API_KEY from one file to another: the occurrence count across the commit is unchanged, so -S says nothing and -G reports it. So -S answers "who introduced this?" and -G answers "who touched anything to do with this?" In practice -S is the one you want, and it's astonishingly effective at the question that comes up most: this line exists, why? git log -S'DEPRECATED_FLAG' --oneline # who added it, who removed it git log -S'password' --all --oneline # across every branch git log -S'foo' -p # with the diffs, to read the context Try it The sandbox has a deploy script that briefly contained a hard-coded password. It's gone from the tip. Find both ends of its life: cat deploy.sh # clean now git log --oneline git log -S'hunter2' --oneline # two commits: the one that added it and the one that removed it git log -S'hunter2' -p # read what actually happened git log -G'PASSWORD' --oneline # a wider net The details (open as much as you like) The two commits -S always finds Searching for a removed string typically returns exactly two commits: the one where the count went 0 → 1, and the one where it went 1 → 0. Which is what makes it the right tool for a leaked credential — you learn when it was exposed and for how long , which is what the incident writeup needs. Add --all so branches and tags are searched too, and --reverse to read oldest-first, which is the natural order for a story. Narrowing it: paths, pathspec magic and -L git l

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 3 · Debugging & forensics Reflog archaeology Your local history of commands, used as evidence. Where was this branch on Tuesday, and what was I standing on when I made that commit? The idea Unit 2 used the reflog as a rescue tool. It's also a record, and reading it as one answers questions the commit graph can't: What did I do to this branch this morning? Every movement, with a reason attached: commit: , rebase (finish): , reset: moving to , checkout: moving from X to Y . Where was main when I branched? main@{n} walks the branch's own log, separately from HEAD's. What was I doing on Tuesday? The selectors take dates: main@{yesterday} , HEAD@{2.hours.ago} , main@{2026-07-01} . The distinction to keep straight: HEAD's log records where you were , and each branch's log records where that branch was . They diverge constantly — every time you commit on another branch, HEAD's log gains an entry and this branch's doesn't. git reflog # HEAD's log: everywhere you've been git reflog show main # main's log: everywhere main has been git reflog --date=iso # with real timestamps rather than @{n} git log -g --oneline # the reflog as commits, so log's flags work That last one is worth remembering: git log -g walks the reflog instead of the parent chain, so you can grep it, patch it, or format it like any other log. Try it The sandbox has a history of moves in it already. Read it as a story: git reflog git reflog show main git log -g --oneline main git reflog --date=iso cat .git/logs/HEAD # the raw file, one line per movement cat .git/logs/refs/heads/main Notice that the file has both the old and new id on every line. That's the property that makes recovery work: the log records what each ref moved away from . The details (open as much as you like) Reading the raw format d1cf19b 587bc61 Ada Rivera <ada@example.com> 1709543400 +0000 commit: fix typo 587bc61 26a5243 Ada Rivera <ada@example.com> 1709543460 +0000 reset: moving to HEAD~2 Old id, new id, who, unix timestamp, timezone

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration --force-with-lease The difference between overwriting your own rewritten branch and silently deleting a colleague's commit. One flag, and it should be the only one you ever type. The idea You rebased a branch you'd already pushed, so your history and the remote's disagree. A normal push is rejected — correctly, because accepting it would make the remote's commits unreachable: ! [rejected] main -> main (non-fast-forward) error: failed to push some refs --force makes it go through. It also makes it go through when the thing you'd be overwriting is a commit your colleague pushed ten minutes ago, which you never fetched and therefore have never seen. That commit becomes unreachable on the remote, and nothing tells anyone. --force-with-lease adds one check: What the lease is Push only if the remote's branch is still exactly where my origin/<branch> says it is. If someone else has pushed since my last fetch, refuse. So it permits exactly the case you meant — I know what's there, I fetched it, and I intend to replace it — and refuses the case you didn't. The rejection reads: ! [rejected] main -> main (stale info) which means "fetch and look again". It costs nothing and it turns a whole class of incident into an error message. Try it The sandbox has a remote that's moved on since you last looked. Watch all three outcomes: git log --oneline --all git push # rejected: non-fast-forward git push --force-with-lease # also rejected: stale info — you haven't fetched git fetch # now you can see what they did git log --oneline --left-right main...origin/main # then decide: rebase onto theirs (keeps their work), or lease-force (replaces it) That middle step is the whole point. --force would have gone through and thrown away the remote's commit without mentioning it. The details (open as much as you like) Why the lease can lie, and the flag that fixes it The lease is checked against your remote-tracking ref, which means it's only as trustworthy as the

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration Hooks Your own code at git's decision points. The mechanism is simple; the interesting part is which hook runs when, and what it's allowed to stop. The idea A hook is an executable file in .git/hooks/ named after the moment it runs. Git runs it, and for some hooks a non-zero exit code cancels the operation . There is no configuration, no registry, and no language requirement — if it's executable, it runs. .git/hooks/pre-commit # before a commit is made — can refuse .git/hooks/commit-msg # gets the message file; can edit or refuse it .git/hooks/pre-push # before objects are sent — can refuse .git/hooks/post-checkout # after a checkout; can't refuse anything .git/hooks/pre-rebase # can refuse to rebase a protected branch The ones that earn their keep: pre-commit format, lint, reject debugger statements or a stray secret. Runs before the commit exists commit-msg enforce a message convention, or append an issue number from the branch name pre-push run the test suite, or refuse to push to main. Gets the refs being pushed on stdin post-checkout / post-merge re-install dependencies when the lock file changed The important limitation: hooks are not cloned . .git/ isn't part of the repository's content, so a hook you write protects only you. Teams distribute them with a committed directory plus git config core.hooksPath .githooks , or a tool like pre-commit that does the wiring. Try it Write a hook that refuses to commit anything containing the word TODO , then watch it work: edit .git/hooks/pre-commit # put a check in it, save echo "x = 1 # TODO fix this" >> count.py git add count.py git commit -m "This should be refused" How hooks work in this sandbox There's no shell in a browser, so a hook here is JavaScript rather than a shell script. The path, the timing, and the veto are real: the file lives at .git/hooks/pre-commit , it runs before the commit is made, and returning false (or throwing) cancels it exactly as a non-zero exit would. h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration Merge strategies and rerere What to do when git can't decide by itself — and how to stop resolving the same conflict every time you rebase. The idea A merge is a three-way merge per file: compare the merge base against each side, take whichever side changed, and stop when both changed the same lines differently. The strategy is how git handles the awkward cases around that. Since git 2.34 the default strategy is ort ("ostensibly recursive's twin"), a rewrite of the old recursive . It's faster, handles renames better, and — usefully — can compute a merge without touching your worktree at all. You rarely need to name a strategy; the options are what matter: -X ours on conflicting hunks , take our side. Everything non-conflicting from both sides is still merged -X theirs the same, favouring theirs -s ours completely different: take our tree wholesale and ignore theirs, while still recording the merge. Used to declare a branch merged without taking its content -X ignore-space-change the answer to a whitespace-only conflict -X patience a different diff algorithm; sometimes untangles a conflict that looks worse than it is The distinction to keep is -X ours versus -s ours . The first resolves conflicts in our favour; the second throws their changes away entirely. They are one character apart and not remotely the same. Try it The sandbox has two branches that both edited the cache size in config.ini . Watch a real conflict, then resolve it three ways: git log --oneline --all git merge tune-cache # conflict — read the markers cat config.ini git merge --abort git merge -X ours tune-cache # our value wins, no prompt git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD git merge -X theirs tune-cache # theirs wins The details (open as much as you like) Reading a conflict properly <<<<<<< HEAD cache = 16 ======= cache = 512 >>>>>>> tune-cache Between <<< and === is yours; between === and >>> is theirs. The markers are a note to you — git doesn't parse them back, so resolv

h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration Refspecs and remotes origin/main is a local file, not a live view of the server. Once that lands, fetch, push and 'ahead 2, behind 1' all stop being mysterious. The idea origin/main is a ref in your repository: refs/remotes/origin/main . It records where origin's main was the last time you fetched. It is a cache, it can be out of date, and nothing about it is live. So three things that look similar are quite different: main your branch origin/main your note of where their branch was at last contact origin's main what's actually on the server right now, which you cannot see without asking "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits" is a comparison against the middle one. It can be wrong the moment a colleague pushes, and git fetch is how you refresh it. This is also why git fetch is safe: it only updates remote-tracking refs and touches nothing of yours. Refspecs A refspec is the mapping that says which ref becomes which: <src>:<dst> Your .git/config contains the fetch refspec that creates all those remote-tracking refs: [remote "origin"] url = git@example.com:project.git fetch = +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/* Read it as: take every branch on the remote and store it under refs/remotes/origin/, allowing non-fast-forward updates (the +). That single line is why origin/* exists at all. git push origin main shorthand for main:refs/heads/main git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/spike push what I'm on, call it spike over there git push origin :old-branch empty source — delete the remote branch git push origin +main the leading plus is --force, written into the refspec git fetch origin main:refs/remotes/origin/main the explicit form of what a plain fetch does Try it The sandbox has a remote whose main has moved on: git remote -v cat .git/config # the refspec is right there git branch -a # remote-tracking refs listed separately git fetch git status # ahead/behind, computed against your local note git log --oneline --left-right main

b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration Stash tricks A stash is a pair of commits with a funny name. Knowing that turns it from a black box into something you can inspect, recover and script. The idea git stash shelves your uncommitted work so your worktree is clean. What it actually does: Makes a commit of the index . Makes a commit of the working tree , with two parents: HEAD and that index commit. Points refs/stash at the second one. Resets your worktree to HEAD. So a stash is ordinary commits, and everything you know about commits applies: you can git show it, diff against it, cherry-pick from it, and recover it from the reflog after dropping it. The "stack" is just refs/stash 's reflog — stash@{2} is a reflog address, exactly like HEAD@{2} . The flags worth knowing -u include untracked files. The default leaves them behind, which is how people lose new files to a subsequent checkout -p choose interactively which hunks to stash — the mirror image of git add -p -k keep the index, so your staged work stays staged and only unstaged changes get shelved -m "…" a message. stash@{3} tells you nothing three days later pop vs apply pop applies and deletes; apply leaves the stash in place. Prefer apply when you're not sure it'll work branch <name> create a branch at the commit the stash was made from, and apply there. The fix for "the stash no longer applies" Try it The sandbox starts dirty. Stash it, look at what got made, and get it back: git status git stash push -u -m "wip: argv handling" git status # clean git stash list git log --oneline refs/stash # it's a commit git show refs/stash # …with your changes in it git stash pop git status # back The details (open as much as you like) Recovering a dropped stash git stash drop removes the ref entry, not the commit. h: The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration Submodules and subtrees A submodule is one tree entry with an unusual mode. Most of its reputation comes from people not knowing that. The idea A submodule is two things, and neither is complicated: A gitlink : a tree entry with mode 160000 , naming one commit in another repository. Not a branch — a commit. A line in .gitmodules saying where to clone that repository from. $ git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree} 100644 blob 8d0e412… README.md 100644 blob 5cff6c5… count.py 160000 commit 3bf7b3a… vendor/parser That's the whole data model. Everything people find awkward follows from the first point: the superproject pins an exact commit, so a clone doesn't get the submodule's content (only its id), your worktree can hold a submodule checkout that doesn't match the pin, and updating means committing a new gitlink in the superproject. b: Unit 4 · Workflow & collaboration Worktrees One object database, several checkouts. The feature that makes stashing and re-cloning mostly unnecessary. The idea A repository has one .git directory and, traditionally, one checkout. git worktree add gives you another checkout, in another directory, sharing the same objects and the same refs: git worktree add ../review feature/parser # check out that branch over there git worktree list git worktree remove ../review What you get, and why it beats the alternatives: versus stashing nothing moves in your main checkout. That division explains every worktree behaviour worth knowing: a commit in one is immediately available in the other (shared objects), each can be on a different branch (own HEAD), and git worktree list can tell you which branch is busy where. Unit 6 · Expert track Big repositories Partial clone, sparse checkout, and the other features that exist because some repositories are far larger than git's original assumptions. The idea Git assumes you want every object in the history and every file in the tree. For most repositories that's right, and it's why clones are self-contained and everything is fast offline. Past a certain size it stops being right, and two independent features relax the two halves of the assumption: Sparse checkout fewer files in your worktree . The index still knows every path; only what you've asked for is written to disk Partial clone fewer objects downloaded . Git fetches the commits and trees, and fetches blobs on demand when something actually needs one They're usually used together, and the combination is what makes a hundred-gigabyte monorepo workable: git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse <url> cd repo git sparse-checkout set services/payments libs/common Now you have the full history graph, a worktree with two directories in it, and blobs arriving only when you check something out or run a diff that needs them. Not runnable in this sandbox Both features are about what gets transferred and written, and this sandbox has no network and a handful of tiny files — so sparse-checkout and --filter aren't implemented here. This page is a map of what exists and when to reach for it; the mechanisms it builds on — the index, trees, refspecs — are all things you've already used. The details The filters, and what each one keeps --filter=blob:none no file contents at all up front. The usual choice: commits and trees are small, blobs are the bulk --filter=blob:limit=1m everything except large blobs — the pragmatic version when a few big files dominate --filter=tree:0 commits only. Very fast, very limited: almost any operation needs a tree, so most things trigger a fetch --depth=1 a shallow clone: recent commits only. b: Unit 6 · Expert track Notes and replace refs Two ways to change what git shows you without changing a single commit. Both are niche, and both are the right answer when you need them. The idea A commit is immutable. Its id is a hash of its content, so adding anything — a review link, a build number, a correction — normally means rewriting it and everything after it. Git has two escape hatches that avoid that, and they work in opposite directions. Notes: attach something alongside git notes add -m "Reviewed by Priya; deployed 2026-07-04" <commit> git log # the note appears under the message git notes show <commit> Notes live in refs/notes/commits : a parallel tree whose paths are commit ids and whose blobs are your text. The commit is untouched, its id is unchanged, and git log knows to look the note up and display it. The catch is distribution. Notes are not fetched or pushed by default — they're a separate ref, and the default refspec doesn't cover it: git push origin refs/notes/commits git fetch origin refs/notes/commits:refs/notes/commits which is why notes work beautifully for CI metadata (a machine can push the ref) and disappointingly for team annotations (a human has to remember). replace: pretend a commit is a different one git replace <old-commit> <new-commit> Creates a ref under refs/replace/<old-id> , and from then on every read of that object transparently gets the other one. History appears to change; nothing was rewritten. Turn it off with --no-replace-objects and the original is right there. The classic use is grafting an old repository onto a new one: convert the history, then replace the new root commit with the old tip, and git log reads through as one continuous story without anyone having to rewrite ten years of commits. h: gc, and what it actually deletes
The details (open as much as you like)
b: Unit 6 · Expert track Packfiles and gc How a repository with a million versions of a file stays small — and the one routine operation that actually deletes your lost commits. The idea Every object starts as a loose object : one zlib-compressed file at .git/objects/ab/cdef… . That's simple and, past a few thousand objects, wasteful — one inode each, no sharing between near-identical versions of the same file. So git periodically bundles them into a packfile : one .pack with the objects, one .idx for finding them by id. Inside a pack, an object may be stored as a delta against another similar object — usually a later version against an earlier one — so a thousand revisions of a file cost roughly one copy plus a thousand small diffs. Two clarifications worth having, because they're the source of most confusion: Deltas are a storage detail, not the data model. Every object is still addressable by its own hash and reconstructible on its own. Git stores snapshots; packs make snapshots cheap. Packing changes nothing you can observe except speed and size. Ids don't change, history doesn't change. gc, and what it actually deletes git gc # pack loose objects, expire reflogs, prune unreachable objects git gc --aggressive # spend much more CPU looking for better deltas. Rarely worth it git count-objects -v # how much loose stuff is lying around The order matters, because it's where lost work finally goes: Reflog entries older than the expiry (90 days reachable, 30 unreachable) are dropped. Objects nothing can reach — including via the remaining reflog — and older than gc.pruneExpire (two weeks) are deleted. So a commit you abandoned today survives roughly two weeks even after its reflog entry goes, and git gc --prune=now is the command that skips the grace period. That's the one to think twice about — it's also the one people paste from the internet when a repository is large. Not runnable in this sandbox This engine only ever writes loose objects; git gc and git repack aren't

Unit 6 · Expert track When not to rewrite The judgement half of this course. Every tool in Unit 2 has a blast radius, and choosing well is mostly about who else is holding the commits. The idea You can now rewrite history several ways. The remaining skill is knowing when the cheaper, additive option is the right one — because a rewrite's cost isn't paid by you, it's paid by whoever already has the commits. One question decides most cases: The question Does anyone else have these commits? If no: rewrite freely, it's free. If yes: the rewrite costs every one of them a recovery procedure, so it needs to be worth that, and it needs to be announced. Local, unpushed Rewrite. amend, rebase -i, reorder, drop. No cost to anyone. Pushed, your branch alone Rewrite, then push --force-with-lease . Standard practice on a pull request branch. Pushed, others are on it Only after telling them, with the exact commands they'll need. Consider whether a follow-up commit would do instead. main, or any long-lived branch Don't. revert gets the same outcome additively. A leaked secret Rotate the credential first. Then rewrite if you like — but the secret is already out, and the rewrite is hygiene, not containment. The habits worth keeping Six things that between them prevent most of the situations this course teaches you to escape from: Commit small and often; tidy before you push. The --fixup + --autosquash loop makes this nearly free, and it moves all your rewriting to before anyone else is affected. Never type --force . Alias it: git config --global alias.pushf "push --force-with-lease" . Set the safe defaults once. pull.ff=only , fetch.prune=true , rerere.enabled=true , rebase.autoSquash=true . Four lines that remove four recurring annoyances. Read the error. Git's rejections are unusually informative — "non-fast-forward", "stale info", "would be overwritten by checkout" each name the exact problem. Check before you rewrite. git log --oneline <upstream>..<branch> shows exactly what a re

One of the four things git stores: a file's contents, a directory listing, a commit, or a tag. The unit of storage in git's database. Every object is stored under the SHA-1 hash of its own contents, which is why the same content is never stored twice and why an id can never disagree with what it names. The four types are blob, tree, commit and tag.

A file's contents, with no name and no history attached. The object type that stores file content. A blob knows nothing about its filename, its permissions or where it sits — a tree supplies all of that. Two identical files anywhere in history are one blob.

A directory listing: names, permissions, and the object each name points at. The object type that gives structure to blobs. Each entry has a mode, a name, and the id of a blob (a file) or another tree (a subdirectory). A commit points at exactly one tree: the complete state of the project at that moment.

A snapshot plus who made it, when, why, and what came before it. An object holding one tree id, zero or more parent commit ids, an author, a committer, and a message. Because the parent ids are part of the hashed content, changing any commit changes every commit after it — the fact that makes rewriting history a rebuild rather than an edit.

A tag that is its own object, with a tagger, a date and a message. Created by `git tag -a`. Unlike a lightweight tag — which is just a ref pointing at a commit — an annotated tag is a fourth kind of object that points at a commit and carries its own metadata, and can be signed.

A name that points at a commit — a branch, a tag, or a remote-tracking name. A file under .git/refs/ (or a line in .git/packed-refs) containing an object id. Branches are refs under refs/heads/, tags under refs/tags/, remote-tracking refs under refs/remotes/. Nearly every git command is, underneath, a way of moving a ref.

A movable name for one commit — and, by following parents, all of its history. A ref under refs/heads/. A branch holds exactly one commit id and moves forward when you commit on it. It is not a container of commits: deleting a branch deletes only the name, which is why the commits survive long enough for the reflog to find them.

Where you are: the commit you have checked out. A symbolic ref in .git/HEAD, normally containing `ref: refs/heads/<branch>` — so it points at a branch, which points at a commit. Committing moves the branch HEAD names, which is how HEAD comes along for the ride.

HEAD points straight at a commit instead of at a branch. The state after `git checkout <commit>`. Commits you make still get created, but no branch moves to include them, so they become unreachable the moment you leave — findable only through the reflog. Rebase and bisect both work in this state deliberately.

A ref that points at another ref instead of at a commit. HEAD is the one you meet daily: it contains a ref name, not an object id. `git symbolic-ref HEAD` reads it; writing it is how `git checkout <branch>` switches branches without touching a single file's content.

The list of exactly what your next commit will contain. A binary file, .git/index, holding a full flat list of paths with the blob id and file stats for each. `git add` writes into it; `git commit` turns it into a tree. It is the third of the three trees — HEAD, the index, the working tree — and most confusing git states are a disagreement between them.

The actual files on disk that you edit. The checked-out copy of your project. Git compares it against the index to tell you what is unstaged, and against HEAD to tell you what has changed since the last commit. `git reset --hard` is the one common command that overwrites it.

A local diary of every position a ref has held. Plain text under .git/logs/: one line per movement of a ref, with the old id, the new id, who moved it and why. It is what makes almost every git accident recoverable, because a commit dropped by reset, rebase or a deleted branch is still named in the log. It is local, private, and expires.

Where HEAD was just before the last big move. A file git writes before operations that move HEAD a long way — reset, rebase, merge, pull. `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` is the one-step undo for the operation you just regretted.

The commit that came before this one. Recorded inside the commit object. A normal commit has one parent, a merge commit has two or more, and the very first commit has none. The first parent is special: it is the branch you were on when you merged, and what `~` and --first-parent follow.

For a merge commit, the branch you were standing on when you merged. Parent number one. `HEAD~3` walks first parents only, and `git log --first-parent` shows the trunk's own story without every merged branch's commits mixed in.

A commit with more than one parent, joining two lines of history. What `git merge` creates when it can't fast-forward. Its tree is the combined result; its parents record both sides, which is what preserves the fact that the two branches existed.

The most recent commit both branches share. The common ancestor a three-way merge measures from: git compares each side against the base to work out what each side changed. `git merge-base a b` prints it.

Combining two versions by looking at what each changed from a common starting point. Compare base→ours and base→theirs. Where only one side changed a region, take that side; where both changed it the same way, take it once; where both changed it differently, that is a conflict. Merge, cherry-pick, revert and every step of rebase are all this operation.

Both sides changed the same lines differently, so git stops and asks you. Git writes both versions into the file between `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers, leaves the path unstaged, and records the in-progress state in .git/. Resolving means editing the file, staging it, and continuing — the marker is a note to you, not a format git understands.

Moving a branch straight up to a commit that already contains it. When your branch tip is an ancestor of what you're merging, git can simply slide the ref forward without making a merge commit. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit anyway; `--ff-only` refuses anything else. The same test decides whether a push is allowed.

The update would drop commits the other side already has, so git refuses. The rejection you get pushing a rewritten branch: the remote's tip is not an ancestor of yours, so accepting your push would make its commits unreachable. Forcing overrides the check; --force-with-lease overrides it safely.

A commit you can reach by walking backwards from another one. Reachability is the relation nearly every git decision rests on: whether a merge can fast-forward, whether a push is safe, whether an object survives gc, what a range means. `git merge-base --is-ancestor a b` tests it.

Some ref can get to it by following parents and trees. An object is reachable if a walk from any ref arrives at it. Reachable objects are permanent; unreachable ones are candidates for garbage collection. Reflog entries also count as starting points, which is exactly why they buy you recovery time.

Still in the database, but no ref can find it any more. What a commit becomes after the branch naming it is deleted or moved off it. It still exists byte-for-byte until git prunes it, which is why recovery is usually possible — via the reflog if it's still listed there, via `git fsck --unreachable` if it isn't.

Unreachable, and nothing else unreachable points at it either. git fsck's word for the tip of an orphaned chain. The distinction from plain 'unreachable' is useful in practice: dangling commits are the heads of lost work, so they are the ones worth looking at first.

Checks the object database and lists what nothing points at. `git fsck` verifies that objects are well-formed and connected, and reports dangling and unreachable ones. With --no-reflogs it ignores the reflog as a starting point, which reveals what is genuinely stranded rather than merely unnamed.

One object stored as one compressed file. The simple storage form: .git/objects/ab/cdef… where the path is the object's own hash. Git periodically bundles many loose objects into a packfile to save space and speed up walks.

Many objects in one file, stored as differences from each other. The compact storage form, with an index file beside it for lookups. Objects in a pack are often kept as deltas against a similar object, which is why a repository with thousands of versions of one file stays small.

Tidies the object database, and eventually deletes what nothing points at. `git gc` packs loose objects and prunes unreachable ones older than a grace period (two weeks by default), after expiring old reflog entries. It is the only routine operation that actually destroys lost commits, which is why recovery is a race you almost always win.

The low-level commands git's own scripts are built from. hash-object, cat-file, write-tree, commit-tree, update-ref and friends: stable, scriptable, and unconcerned with being friendly. The commands you use daily — 'porcelain' — are convenience layers over these.

Replace the last commit with a new one. `git commit --amend` does not edit a commit — it cannot, because a commit's id is its content. It builds a new commit with the same parent and moves the branch to it, leaving the old one unreachable and recoverable from the reflog.

Building replacement commits and pointing the branch at them. What amend, rebase, cherry-pick and filter-repo all do. The originals are never modified; they are abandoned. This is why rewriting is safe on your own branch and rude on a shared one: everyone else's history still contains the commits you abandoned.

Replay your commits on top of a different starting point. For each commit in a range, git works out what it changed and applies that change onto a new base, creating a new commit with a new id. The result is a linear history that looks as if you had started from the newer base — a story that never actually happened, told more clearly.

A rebase where you get to edit the list of steps first. `git rebase -i` writes a todo list to .git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo and opens it in your editor. Changing a line's command — pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, exec — changes what happens to that commit. It is a small programming language for history.

The file that says what an interactive rebase will do, step by step. .git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo. Git reads it top to bottom, and rewrites it as it goes, so `--continue` after a conflict simply resumes where the file says it got to. Because it is a file, you can inspect it mid-rebase.

Fold a commit into the one before it, keeping both messages. A rebase todo command. The two commits become one whose tree is the later state and whose message you get to edit, combining both. Use fixup instead when the second message is just 'oops'.

Fold a commit into the one before it and throw its message away. Like squash without the message merge. `git commit --fixup=<commit>` writes a commit whose subject is `fixup! <that commit's subject>`, so a later `rebase --autosquash` knows where it belongs without you reordering anything.

Moves every fixup! commit under the commit it names, automatically. `git rebase -i --autosquash` reorders the todo list before showing it to you: each `fixup!`/`squash!` commit is placed directly after its target with its command changed. With rebase.autoSquash=true it is the default, and reviewing a branch becomes a two-command habit.

Says where the replayed commits should land, separately from which ones they are. `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [branch]` splits the two questions rebase normally conflates: `<upstream>..branch` chooses the commits, `<newbase>` chooses the destination. The tool for lifting a branch off the wrong parent.

Copy one commit's change onto the branch you're on. Applies the difference a commit made and commits the result — a new commit, with a new id, the same author and a new committer. `-x` records which commit it came from, which is the difference between a traceable backport and a mystery.

A new commit that undoes an old one, leaving the old one in place. The safe undo for history other people already have: it adds, rather than rewrites. `git revert <commit>` applies that commit's change backwards. Reverting a merge needs -m to say which side to keep.

Move the current branch, and optionally the index and your files with it. `--soft` moves the branch only; `--mixed` (the default) also makes the index match; `--hard` also overwrites the working tree. Untracked files are never touched by any of them. Nothing is deleted from the database, so the reflog can undo it.

Binary search through history for the commit that broke something. You mark one commit good and one bad; git checks out the middle one and asks. Each answer halves the range, so a thousand commits take about ten tests. `git bisect run <script>` does the answering for you when the test can be automated.

Shows which commit last touched each line of a file. Useful, and misleading by default: a rename or a move makes every line look new. `-M` follows lines moved within a file, `-C` follows lines copied from other files in the same commit, and `-L` limits the search to a range of lines.

Searches history for the commits where a string appeared or disappeared. `git log -S<string>` reports commits that changed how many times the string occurs — the ones that added or removed it. `-G<regex>` is broader: every commit whose diff mentions it at all. -S answers 'who introduced this', -G answers 'who touched this'.

Shelves your uncommitted changes so you can come back to them. Records the working tree and index as commits parented off HEAD, pointed at by the refs/stash ref, then cleans your worktree. Because they are ordinary commits, a lost stash is recoverable through the stash reflog. `-u` includes untracked files, which the default deliberately doesn't.

A second checkout of the same repository, in another directory. `git worktree add` gives you another working tree and another HEAD sharing one object database and one set of refs. Cheaper than a clone, and unlike stashing it lets you have two branches genuinely open at once. Two worktrees cannot have the same branch checked out.

A rule saying which ref maps to which, when you fetch or push. `<src>:<dst>`, optionally prefixed with + to allow a non-fast-forward update. `refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*` is the fetch refspec that fills in your remote-tracking refs; `git push origin :old` has an empty source, which is how a push deletes a remote branch.

Your local note of where a branch on the remote was, last time you looked. A ref under refs/remotes/, such as refs/remotes/origin/main. You never commit on it; fetch updates it. It is a cache, and its being a cache is the whole point: --force-with-lease compares against it to detect that someone else pushed.

The remote branch your branch is set up to compare itself against. Configured as branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge, and written `@{u}` or `@{upstream}`. It is what makes `git status` able to say 'ahead 2, behind 1' without you naming a branch.

Force-push, but only if the remote is still where you last saw it. Compares the remote's current tip against your remote-tracking ref and refuses if they differ. This is the difference between overwriting your own rewritten branch and silently deleting a colleague's commit — which is exactly what plain --force does.

Remembers how you resolved a conflict and replays it next time. 'Reuse recorded resolution'. With rerere.enabled, git records the conflict's pre-image and your resolution under .git/rr-cache/ and reapplies it automatically when it sees the same conflict again — which happens constantly when you rebase a long-lived branch repeatedly.

A pointer to one specific commit of another repository. A tree entry with mode 160000 — a 'gitlink' — naming a commit id, plus a .gitmodules file saying where to clone it from. The superproject records which commit, not which branch, which is the source of both its precision and its reputation.

Another project's files copied into a subdirectory of yours, history and all. The alternative to a submodule: the files are really in your tree, so a clone needs nothing extra, at the cost of a bigger repository and a more involved update procedure.

The number in a tree entry saying what kind of thing it is. 100644 a file, 100755 an executable file, 120000 a symlink, 040000 a subdirectory, 160000 a submodule. Git stores no other permissions — the executable bit is the only one that survives a clone.

A script git runs at a particular moment, which can refuse to continue. An executable in .git/hooks/ named for its moment: pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push, post-checkout. A non-zero exit stops the operation. Hooks are not cloned, which is why teams distribute them separately.

Having only part of the repository's files in your working tree. The index knows about every path, but only the patterns you list get written to disk. Combined with a partial clone (which also skips downloading the blobs you don't need) it is how very large repositories stay workable.

Extra text attached to a commit without changing it. `git notes` stores annotations in refs/notes/commits, keyed by the commit they describe, so `git log` can display them. Because the commit itself is untouched, its id doesn't change — the only way to add to a commit after the fact.
say head. the commit you have checked out — normally via the branch you're on
say at. exactly the same thing as HEAD, two fewer keystrokes
say rev tilde. the first parent of <rev>. HEAD~ is the commit before HEAD
say rev tilde three. walk back 3 commits, always taking the first parent. HEAD~3 is three commits ago on this line of history
say rev caret. the same as <rev>~ for an ordinary commit: its first parent
say rev caret two. the second parent of a merge commit — the branch that was merged in. Only merge commits have one
say rev caret brace tree. the tree object of that commit, rather than the commit itself. HEAD^{tree} is the root directory of your last commit
say rev caret brace commit. follow tags until you reach an actual commit. Useful because an annotated tag is an object in its own right
say colon slash text. the newest commit whose message contains that text. :/fix typo finds it without you looking up an id
say the sha, or the hash. any unambiguous prefix of a full 40-character id — usually 7 characters is plenty

t: HEAD@{1} — at brace n — the nth reflog entry
b: say head at brace one. where HEAD pointed one move ago. HEAD@{0} is now, HEAD@{1} is before your last command — the undo button's address
say main at brace two. where the branch main pointed two of its own movements ago. Each ref has a separate log, so main@{2} and HEAD@{2} usually differ
say at brace minus one. the branch you were on before this one — what `git checkout -` uses
say at brace you, or at upstream. the remote-tracking branch your branch is set to compare against, usually origin/<same name>
say at brace push. the ref `git push` would update — the same as @{u} in ordinary setups, different under triangular workflows
say orig head. where HEAD was before the last big move (reset, rebase, merge, pull). `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` undoes it

t: A..B — two dots — in B but not A
b: say A dot dot B. the commits reachable from B that aren't reachable from A. main..feature is 'my branch's own commits'

t: A...B — three dots — in either but not both
b: say A dot dot dot B. the symmetric difference: everything either side has that the other doesn't. With --left-right, git marks which side each commit came from
say not A, B. the long form of a range: include B, exclude A. Takes any number of each, unlike ..
say rev caret bang. the commit and none of its ancestors — a range containing exactly one commit
say first parent. when walking, only ever follow parent number one — the trunk's own story, without the commits merged into it
say refs heads main. what the branch 'main' is really called. Branches live under refs/heads/
say refs tags v one point oh. tags live under refs/tags/ and, by convention, don't move
say refs remotes origin main. your local note of where origin's main was when you last fetched. Written origin/main for short
say refs stash. the ref pointing at your most recent stash. Its reflog holds the older ones — which is why a dropped stash is recoverable
say source colon destination. push or fetch the ref on the left into the ref on the right. `git push origin main:main` is the explicit form of the everyday push
say plus source colon destination. update even if it isn't a fast-forward. This is what --force does, written into the refspec itself
say colon destination. push nothing into that ref, which deletes it. `git push origin :old-branch` removes the remote branch
say wildcard refspec. every branch on the remote becomes a remote-tracking ref locally. This line in .git/config is why origin/* exists
say dash dash. everything after this is a path, not a revision. `git checkout -- file` means the file, even if a branch shares its name
say rev colon path. the blob for that path in that commit. `git show HEAD~2:src/app.py` prints the old version without checking anything out
say colon paren exclude. everything except this. `git log -- . ':(exclude)*.lock'` skips the noisy files
say one hundred six forty-four. a regular, non-executable file. The commonest thing in any tree
say one hundred seven fifty-five. a regular file with the executable bit set. The only permission git records
say one twenty thousand. the 'file' content is the path it points at
say forty thousand. the entry is another tree object
say one sixty thousand. a 'gitlink': the entry names a commit in another repository rather than any content in this one
